3.1 Epidemiology.summary: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), presenting as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE), is the third most frequent acute cardiovascular syndrome after myocardial infarction and stroke. Reported annual incidence rates: PE 39–115 per 100,000; DVT 53–162 per 100,000. Incidence of VTE is about eight times higher in individuals aged ≥80 years than in the fifth decade. Longitudinal studies show rising PE incidence over time. Estimated annual EU costs up to €8.5 billion. PE may cause ~300,000 deaths/year in the US. In a six-country European population (454.4 million) >370,000 deaths were related to VTE in 2004; of these, 34% died suddenly or within a few hours, 59% were diagnosed after death, and only 7% of patients who died early were correctly diagnosed with PE before death. Time-trend analyses suggest decreasing case fatality rates for acute PE, likely due to better therapies and guideline adherence, though overdiagnosis of subsegmental/non-existent PE may falsely lower case fatality by inflating the denominator. Figure 1 summarizes global trends. Pediatric data: annual VTE incidence among hospitalized children 53–157 per 100,000 and 1.4–4.9 per 100,000 in the community overall.
key_points: VTE (DVT/PE) is the third most frequent acute cardiovascular syndrome globally.
Higher incidence in older adults (≈8× in ≥80 years vs fifth decade).
Rising PE incidence over time; decreasing case fatality rates likely from improved care but may be affected by overdiagnosis.
Substantial mortality and economic burden (EU estimate up to €8.5 billion).

VTE is considered the consequence of interaction between patient-related (usually permanent) risk factors and setting-related (usually temporary) risk factors. Categorization of temporary and permanent risk factors is important for risk assessment.
